name: Costa Rica
snapshot: Laura Fernández, a protégé of the outgoing populist president, won in the first round in February 2026 on a promise to fight the rising drug violence.
culture: "Pura vida" is Costa Rica's greeting, farewell and philosophy. The country abolished its army in 1948 and spent the money on schools and hospitals, which it celebrates every December. A quarter of its land is protected, and eco-tourism is central to national identity. Gallo pinto, rice and beans, starts the day.
society: Costa Rica has one of Latin America's highest life expectancies and nearly all its electricity comes from renewables. Medical device factories and tourism drive the economy. But homicides have hit record highs as Caribbean ports became transit points for cocaine, unsettling a country used to being the region's safe haven.
situation: Costa Rica abolished its army in 1948 and built a reputation as Central America's peaceful, green, stable democracy. That image has been cracking. Cocaine trafficking through its Pacific ports has pushed murders to record highs, and in 2026 voters chose the candidate promising to govern like the man who had broken its political habits.

On 1 February, Laura Fernández, a 39-year-old political scientist who had served as a minister under the outgoing president, won in the first round with about 48 percent, more than enough to avoid a runoff, against 33 percent for the traditional National Liberation Party (AP via Ottumwa Courier). She campaigned as the openly declared "heir" of President Rodrigo Chaves, a combative populist barred from re-election, and supporters chanted "Long live Chaves!" at her rallies (Confidencial). She is only the second woman to lead Costa Rica, after Laura Chinchilla. Her Pueblo Soberano party became the largest bloc in congress, with about 31 of 57 seats, the biggest governing caucus since 1982, but short of the supermajority Chaves wanted in order to name Supreme Court judges (NPR via WGCU). Turnout jumped to 69 percent. Costa Rica's institutions are now testing whether they can absorb a populist movement without bending.
power: A presidential republic. The president is directly elected for four years, needing 40 percent to avoid a runoff, and cannot serve consecutive terms. The 57-seat Legislative Assembly is unicameral. There is no army.
holders: President Laura Fernández (Pueblo Soberano), in office since 8 May 2026.
